You’ll guide them with clarity and compassion - no cold calls or pushy tactics, just meaningful conversations that help people make one of life’s most important decisions with confidence.</p> <p>This is a sales role: you're responsible for helping families make confident decisions and guiding them to a close - always with genuine care, never pressure. Depending on team needs and performance, this role may include a mix of inbound sales conversations, returning lead follow-up, and support work that helps the broader sales process run smoothly.</p> <p><em>A quick note, because many candidates wonder about it:&nbsp;</em>People often assume this work is emotionally heavy, but our team consistently finds it deeply meaningful and surprisingly uplifting. The role is rooted in hospitality, clarity, and human connection, not sadness. Rather than feeling heavy, the work offers a unique sense of purpose as part of a modern, compassionate company transforming an outdated industry and bringing dignity, transparency, and warmth to families across the country.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h3>Grow Your Career</h3> <p>Most teammates begin in our&nbsp;<strong>Second Call Representative</strong>&nbsp;role, a customer-facing sales position where you'll build product expertise, close deals, and develop our consultative sales approach.</p> <p>High-performing Day Shift reps may become eligible to join our&nbsp;<strong>First Call Representative</strong>&nbsp;team after approximately three months. First Call Reps receive more inbound opportunities and move to an uncapped performance-based compensation plan tied directly to dollars sold, creating meaningful upside for top performers.</p> <p>Eligibility for the First Call team is based on sustained performance, including strong conversion results, customer experience, workflow accuracy, and overall reliability.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <h3>What You’ll Do</h3> <ul> <li> <p>Handle warm inbound leads and support families through the sales process with clarity, empathy, and strong follow-through.</p> </li> <li> <p>Guide families through cremation options, helping them make a confident decision when possible and ensuring thoughtful follow-up when more time is needed.</p> </li> <li> <p>Manage returning leads and follow-up conversations across phone, text, and email so no family falls through the cracks.</p> </li> <li> <p>Contribute to queue coverage, sales activities, and related support workflows that improve the overall customer experience.</p> </li> <li> <p>Hit performance targets while maintaining strong conversion outcomes and quality scores.</p> </li> <li> <p>Move fluently across our stack - HubSpot, Aircall, GSuite, Slack, and our case management system.</p> </li> </ul> <h3>Requirements</h3> <ul> <li>Must currently reside in Latin America, the Caribbean, or the Philippines.</li> <li> <p>2+ years of sales experience with a track record of meeting or exceeding individual targets - managing the full sales cycle and closing, ideally consumer (B2C) sales over the phone.</p> </li> <li> <p>Strong sales instincts and phone presence: you can guide a live conversation toward a confident decision, handle objections naturally, and build trust with families while balancing sales conversations with follow-up and support work.</p> </li> <li> <p>Clear spoken and written English; you explain options simply and warmly.</p> </li> <li> <p>Self-driven and results-focused: you track where you stand against your target and adjust when you're behind. Emotionally steady and highly coachable</p> </li> <li> <p>Comfortable working independently and managing a consistent follow-up rhythm.</p> </li> <li> <p>Familiarity with HubSpot or comparable CRMs (Salesforce, Zoho, etc.).</p> </li> <li> <p>A home setup that supports the work - see our&nbsp;<a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Iap_48WyBpiBL098Y7EC15a26syH7C9vfeXk_FAcOVI/edit?usp=sharing">tech requirements</a>&nbsp;for details.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Bonus Points</p> <ul> <li> <p>Experience selling in high-trust categories (insurance, healthcare, travel, etc.).</p> </li> <li> <p>Spanish fluency — many of the families we serve speak it.</p> </li> </ul> <h3>Details:</h3> <ul> <li> <p>Remote, full-time</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Compensation:</strong> $6-$14 OTE, depending on your location and local market.</p> <ul> <li> <p><em>Competitive base pay plus monthly performance bonuses.</em></p> </li> <li> <p><em>The advertised OTE reflects expected earnings in your starting role. Top performers who advance to our&nbsp;<strong>First Call Representative</strong>&nbsp;team move to an uncapped performance-based compensation plan with significantly higher earning potential.</em></p> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <ul> <li> <p><strong>Tools</strong>: HubSpot (CRM), Aircall (phone), Slack, and our case management system</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Schedule:</strong></p> <ul> <li> <p>Full-time, 8-hour shifts on a consistent weekly schedule</p> </li> <li> <p>Days: Monday–Friday, Tuesday–Saturday, or Sunday–Thursday</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>(weekend availability a plus)</strong></p> </li> <li> <p>Available shift windows:</p> <ul> <li> <p>AM (start 6–8am EST)</p> </li> <li> <p>PM (start 1–4pm EST)</p> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> </li> </ul> <h3>Why You’ll Love Working With Us:</h3> <ul> <li> <p><strong>We’re a real business, built to last.</strong>&nbsp;We’ve proven our model in LA and became the largest independent funeral home in California in less than two years. We are hiring a hands-on performance creative operator to work directly with the owners on our internal portfolio of brands.</p> <p><strong>This is not a conventional graphic-design role.</strong> We need someone who understands why Meta ads convert and can personally turn that understanding into high-quality static and video creative using current AI production tools.</p> <p>You may come from dropshipping, affiliate marketing, DTC, a performance agency, or a creative media-buying background. We care more about commercial judgment, production ability, speed, and proof of work than polished credentials.</p> <h3>The work</h3> <p>You will use and help improve our internal Creative Cockpit. It takes a brand from research and foundational strategy through campaign creation, production, review, and delivery. For each brand, the system holds brand assets and voice, customer language and audience psychology, pains and desires, necessary beliefs, competitor intelligence, awareness levels, angles, hooks, offer context, prior creative, winners, and performance signals.</p> <p>Your job is to turn that intelligence into creative that can sell.</p> <ul> <li>Read campaign briefs, audience research, voice-of-customer material, and brand strategy documents.</li> <li>Decide what each batch should test and why.</li> <li>Source and analyse strong visual and structural references.</li> <li>Develop angles, hooks, scripts, concepts, storyboards, and landing-page direction.</li> <li>Personally produce static ads and short-form video ads.</li> <li>Use AI image, video, voice, and editing tools at a high level.</li> <li>Create meaningful variants without producing repetitive AI slop.</li> <li>Review work for persuasion, visual quality, brand fit, platform fit, and compliance.</li> <li>Refine weak generations rather than accepting the first output.</li> <li>Package approved assets for launch and document what each concept tests.</li> <li>Read results and use the learning to plan the next batch.</li> </ul> <h3>What you must be good at</h3> <ul> <li>Direct-response advertising and Meta creative strategy</li> <li>Audience psychology and voice-of-customer interpretation</li> <li>Awareness levels, hooks, angles, mechanisms, objections, offers, and message-market fit</li> <li>Understanding when an ad should lead to a PDP, advertorial, listicle, quiz, or sales page</li> <li>Static ad, UGC, and short-form video production</li> <li>Visual-reference analysis and controlled recreation</li> <li>Current AI image and video workflows using tools such as Seedance, Google Flow/Omni, Nano Banana/Gemini, GPT Image, Higgsfield, Kling, Sora, Veo, or comparable tools</li> <li>Editing, compositing, pacing, captions, sound, and final polish</li> <li>Fast, organised batch production</li> <li>Reading creative performance and choosing the next test</li> </ul> <h3>You are probably not right for this role if</h3> <ul> <li>Your portfolio is mostly branding, organic social content, or attractive design without performance context.</li> <li>You call every asset “scroll-stopping” but cannot explain the audience belief or conversion mechanism.</li> <li>You are a strategist who depends on other people to make the work.</li> <li>You are a tool operator who needs someone else to provide every hook, angle, script, and decision.</li> <li>You use one prompt, accept the first output, and call it AI production.</li> <li>You cannot show exactly what you personally contributed to portfolio examples.</li> <li>You dislike volume, iteration, testing, or direct feedback.</li> </ul> <h3>What success looks like</h3> <p>Within 30 days, you can understand our strategy packs and operating system, take a structured brief from research to finished assets with limited supervision, produce a useful weekly mix of static and video concepts, explain the reason for every important decision, maintain quality while moving quickly, and suggest practical improvements to the workflow.</p> <h3>Compensation</h3> <p>The role begins with a fully paid 30-day working trial at <strong>USD $2,000</strong>. If the fit is strong, it becomes a long-term full-time position expected to pay <strong>USD $2,000 to $3,000 per month</strong>, based on demonstrated level, with additional performance upside available for an exceptional long-term operator.</p> <p>We care about ability, English comprehension, reliability, some overlap with our working hours, and quality of output.</p> <h3>How to apply</h3> <p><strong>Do not send a generic cover letter.</strong> Message Simon on WhatsApp at <strong>+353 86 349 5073</strong> and begin with: <strong>I make the work.</strong></p> <ol> <li>Send three Meta ads you personally made or materially directed.</li> <li>For each example, state exactly what you did and explain the audience, angle, hook, and intended next step in the funnel.</li> <li>Share any useful performance context you are permitted to disclose. Redacted evidence is acceptable.</li> <li>Show one weak or failed creative and explain what you learned or changed.</li> <li>List the AI tools you use in real production and explain your normal workflow from reference to finished asset.</li> <li>Send a Loom of no more than five minutes. Choose one Meta ad you respect, explain why it works, and describe the next three variants you would test.</li> <li>State your location, timezone, availability, and expected monthly compensation after the trial.</li> </ol> <p>Applications without the requested evidence will not be reviewed. Shortlisted candidates will complete a small paid practical exercise before the 30-day trial.</p> <p><strong>To apply:</strong> <a href="https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/icarus-digital-marketing-performance-creative-strategist-and-ai-producer">https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/icarus-digital-marketing-performance-creative-strategist-and-ai-producer</a></p&g

We are hiring a hands-on performance creative operator to work directly with the owners on our internal portfolio of brands.</p> <p><strong>This is not a conventional graphic-design role.</strong> We need someone who understands why Meta ads convert and can personally turn that understanding into high-quality static and video creative using current AI production tools.</p> <p>You may come from dropshipping, affiliate marketing, DTC, a performance agency, or a creative media-buying background. We care more about commercial judgment, production ability, speed, and proof of work than polished credentials.</p> <h3>The work</h3> <p>You will use and help improve our internal Creative Cockpit. It takes a brand from research and foundational strategy through campaign creation, production, review, and delivery. For each brand, the system holds brand assets and voice, customer language and audience psychology, pains and desires, necessary beliefs, competitor intelligence, awareness levels, angles, hooks, offer context, prior creative, winners, and performance signals.</p> <p>Your job is to turn that intelligence into creative that can sell.</p> <ul> <li>Read campaign briefs, audience research, voice-of-customer material, and brand strategy documents.</li> <li>Decide what each batch should test and why.</li> <li>Source and analyse strong visual and structural references.</li> <li>Develop angles, hooks, scripts, concepts, storyboards, and landing-page direction.</li> <li>Personally produce static ads and short-form video ads.</li> <li>Use AI image, video, voice, and editing tools at a high level.</li> <li>Create meaningful variants without producing repetitive AI slop.</li> <li>Review work for persuasion, visual quality, brand fit, platform fit, and compliance.</li> <li>Refine weak generations rather than accepting the first output.</li> <li>Package approved assets for launch and document what each concept tests.</li> <li>Read results and use the learning to plan the next batch.</li> </ul> <h3>What you must be good at</h3> <ul> <li>Direct-response advertising and Meta creative strategy</li> <li>Audience psychology and voice-of-customer interpretation</li> <li>Awareness levels, hooks, angles, mechanisms, objections, offers, and message-market fit</li> <li>Understanding when an ad should lead to a PDP, advertorial, listicle, quiz, or sales page</li> <li>Static ad, UGC, and short-form video production</li> <li>Visual-reference analysis and controlled recreation</li> <li>Current AI image and video workflows using tools such as Seedance, Google Flow/Omni, Nano Banana/Gemini, GPT Image, Higgsfield, Kling, Sora, Veo, or comparable tools</li> <li>Editing, compositing, pacing, captions, sound, and final polish</li> <li>Fast, organised batch production</li> <li>Reading creative performance and choosing the next test</li> </ul> <h3>You are probably not right for this role if</h3> <ul> <li>Your portfolio is mostly branding, organic social content, or attractive design without performance context.</li> <li>You call every asset “scroll-stopping” but cannot explain the audience belief or conversion mechanism.</li> <li>You are a strategist who depends on other people to make the work.</li> <li>You are a tool operator who needs someone else to provide every hook, angle, script, and decision.</li> <li>You use one prompt, accept the first output, and call it AI production.</li> <li>You cannot show exactly what you personally contributed to portfolio examples.</li> <li>You dislike volume, iteration, testing, or direct feedback.</li> </ul> <h3>What success looks like</h3> <p>Within 30 days, you can understand our strategy packs and operating system, take a structured brief from research to finished assets with limited supervision, produce a useful weekly mix of static and video concepts, explain the reason for every important decision, maintain quality while moving quickly, and suggest practical improvements to the workflow.</p> <h3>Compensation</h3> <p>The role begins with a fully paid 30-day working trial at <strong>USD $2,000</strong>. If the fit is strong, it becomes a long-term full-time position expected to pay <strong>USD $2,000 to $3,000 per month</strong>, based on demonstrated level, with additional performance upside available for an exceptional long-term operator.</p> <p>We care about ability, English comprehension, reliability, some overlap with our working hours, and quality of output.</p> <h3>How to apply</h3> <p><strong>Do not send a generic cover letter.</strong> Message Simon on WhatsApp at <strong>+353 86 349 5073</strong> and begin with: <strong>I make the work.</strong></p> <ol> <li>Send three Meta ads you personally made or materially directed.</li> <li>For each example, state exactly what you did and explain the audience, angle, hook, and intended next step in the funnel.</li> <li>Share any useful performance context you are permitted to disclose. Redacted evidence is acceptable.</li> <li>Show one weak or failed creative and explain what you learned or changed.</li> <li>List the AI tools you use in real production and explain your normal workflow from reference to finished asset.</li> <li>Send a Loom of no more than five minutes. Choose one Meta ad you respect, explain why it works, and describe the next three variants you would test.</li> <li>State your location, timezone, availability, and expected monthly compensation after the trial.</li> </ol> <p>Applications without the requested evidence will not be reviewed. Shortlisted candidates will complete a small paid practical exercise before the 30-day trial.</p> <p><strong>To apply:</strong> <a href="https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/icarus-digital-marketing-performance-creative-strategist-and-ai-producer">https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/icarus-digital-marketing-performance-creative-strategist-and-ai-producer</a></p&g
newContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 Customer.io: Mid-Market Account Executive, Americas Anywhere in the World Sales and Marketing Full-Time <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Americas Remote </p> <p>Hello, I’m Jacob, Senior Sales Manager at&nbsp;<a href="http://customer.io/">Customer.io</a>! We're expanding our sales team in the <strong>United States</strong> and seeking motivated and successful Account Executives at the Mid-Market level to join us! This role offers a unique opportunity to take your sales career to the next level, with potential for upward mobility.</p> <p>As an Account Executive, you’ll represent&nbsp;<a href="http://customer.io/">Customer.io</a>&nbsp;to prospective customers and drive growth within key market segments. This is a full-cycle sales role (prospect, demo, close), where you'll be fielding both inbound and outbound demand.</p> <h3>About&nbsp;<a href="http://customer.io/">Customer.io</a></h3> <p>Over 8,000 companies — from scrappy startups to global brands — use our platform to send billions of emails, push notifications, in-app messages, and SMS every day.&nbsp;<a href="http://customer.io/">Customer.io</a>&nbsp;powers automated communication that people actually want to receive. We help teams send smarter, more relevant messages using real-time behavioral data.</p> <h3><strong>Responsibilities</strong>:</h3> <ul> <li><strong>Pipeline Development and Management</strong>: Build and manage a pipeline through self-sourced leads and SDR-supported leads to drive new customer acquisition.</li> <li><strong>Full-Cycle Sales Execution</strong>: Lead the entire sales process from prospecting and discovery through demo and closing, focusing on new business acquisition within targeted accounts.</li> <li><strong>Customer Needs Analysis and Solution Alignment</strong>: Conduct discovery calls to understand customer business challenges and goals. Position&nbsp;<a href="http://customer.io/">Customer.io</a>'s solutions to meet these needs effectively.</li> <li><strong>Collaboration and Cross-Functional Feedback</strong>: Work closely with the SDR team for lead quality feedback and collaborate with Customer Success and Technical Support for a smooth hand-off post-sale.</li> <li><strong>Performance Tracking and Reporting</strong>: Own and report on individual sales metrics, including pipeline status and progress towards targets, to support informed decision-making.</li> </ul> <h3><strong>Qualifications</strong>:</h3> <ul> <li><strong>Experience:</strong>&nbsp;2+ years of experience in full-cycle B2B SaaS or MarTech sales, handling mid-market accounts</li> <li><strong>Location:</strong>&nbsp;We are currently hiring for positions based in the UK, Ireland, and the Americas (Canada and the USA). Candidates must be located in one of these regions to be considered for the role.</li> <li><strong>B2B SaaS or MarTech Experience</strong>: Proven success in&nbsp;<strong>new customer acquisition</strong>&nbsp;and closing deals within the B2B SaaS space, preferably MarTech</li> <li><strong>Sales Methodology</strong>: Familiarity with MEDDPICC or a similar framework that supports consultative selling and discovery to close.</li> <li><strong>Communication Skills</strong>: Excellent written and verbal communication skills, with a professional and engaging presence to build rapport with new prospects.</li> <li><strong>Problem Solving</strong>: Strong ability to identify customer business needs and position relevant solutions effectively to drive acquisition</li> <li><strong>Deal Focus</strong>: Primarily handles mid-market accounts with shorter sales cycles and lower ACV deals</li> <li><strong>Support</strong>: Works closely with our SDR team for lead generation, with a balance between inbound and self-sourced opportunities</li> <li><strong>Responsibilities</strong>: <ul> <li>Engage in high-volume prospecting, cold and warm outreach</li> <li>Manage the full sales cycle for deals typically under $50,000 ACV</li> <li>Drive growth within mid-sized clients, nurturing relationships and uncovering business needs</li> </ul> </li> </ul> <h3>Compensation &amp; Benefits</h3> <p>We believe in transparency. We are offering a compensation package of $95,000 base + $95,000 variable for a total $190,000 OTE USD (or equivalent in local currency), subject to market rate adjustment.</p> <p>We know our people are what make us great, and we’re committed to taking great care of them. Our inclusive benefits package supports your well-being and growth, including&nbsp;<strong>100% coverage of medical, dental, vision, mental health, and supplemental insurance premiums for you and your family</strong>. We also offer&nbsp;<strong>16 weeks paid parental leave, unlimited PTO</strong>, stipends for remote work and wellness, a professional development budget, and more.</p> <p><a href="https://customer.io/careers#:~:text=our%20collective%20success.-,BENEFITS,-Our%C2%A0">See full benefits here →</a></p> <h3>Our Process</h3> <p>No gotchas, no trick questions - just a clear, human process designed to help both of us make an informed decision.</p> <ol> <li>30-minute video call with a Recruiter</li> <li>45-minute video call with the Hiring Manager</li> <li>60-minute Mock Call w/ the Hiring Team</li> </ol> <p>All final candidates will be asked to complete a background check and employment verifications as part of our pre-employment process.</p> <p><a href="http://customer.io/">Customer.io</a>&nbsp;recognizes the stifling impact of systemic injustice on diverse communities. We commit to using our influence to increase inclusion and equity within the tech industry. We strive to build an inclusive team culture, implement bias-free hiring practices, and develop community partnerships to expand our global impact.</p> <p>Zoom is the only video conference platform that we use, virtual interviews will be conducted using the video capability (i.e., not via the chat), and offers will be extended in writing on official <a href="http://Customer.io">Customer.io</a> letterhead. Please be vigilant in all of your job search activity, and if you have any questions please contact&nbsp;<a href="mailto:jobs@customer.io">jobs@customer.io</a>.</p> <h3><strong>Join us!</strong></h3> <p>Check out our&nbsp;<a href="https://customer.io/careers/">careers page</a>&nbsp;for more information about why you should&nbsp;<a href="https://customer.io/about/">come work with us!</a>&nbsp;We are passionate about our core values of Empathy, Transparency, Responsibility, and Awkwardness and are looking for new coworkers to share and build that passion!</p> <p></p> <p><strong>To apply:</strong> <a href="https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/customer-io-mid-market-account-executive-americas">https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/customer-io-mid-market-account-executive-americas

However, data shows it is a common path, especially as of late with the rise of deep-pocketed, ultra-high-valuation unicorns. So far this year, more than 500 seed- or venture-backed private companies across the globe have sold to other private, venture-backed companies, per Crunchbase data. The most prolific acquirers include many of the most famous and valuable unicorns, including OpenAI , Databricks and Anthropic . Overall, the pace of dealmaking in 2026 looks relatively flat 1 Reported deal counts are down slightly this year from the comparable period, but are likely to even out more over time as some acquisitions, particularly smaller deals, are added to the dataset weeks or months after they close. 2 compared to last year. That’s not entirely surprising given that overall market conditions haven’t changed dramatically. The number of tech startup IPOs remains below normal. Hot venture-backed AI companies are still sustaining unheard-of valuations . And the rise of megarounds means favored startup acquirers are flush with cash. Startups buying startups in recent years In total, at least 440 funded startups sold to other startups in the first half of this year. The second half is shaping up to be a bit slower, meanwhile, with fewer than 100 deals so far. For a more expansive chronological view, below we charted startup M&A deal counts by half-year beginning in 2021. The pace of M&A dealmaking peaked about four years ago and fell afterward, in tandem with a broader dip in startup investment. But activity has picked up over the past couple of years with the rise in AI investment. Startups that buy a lot of other startups A few startups have proven particularly acquisitive. The standout in this category is probably OpenAI, which has acquired eight startups this year, most of them seed- or early-stage companies. To date, the generative AI giant has bought at least 19 companies, per Crunchbase data. Anthropic has also been a busy buyer. It’s snapped up at least five startups so far this year, including the $400 million purchase of AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio . In the fintech space, meanwhile, MoonPay has been on an M&A spree. The crypto transactions platform acquired five funded startups focused on cryptocurrency or blockchain between April and July. Others with multiple funded startup M&A deals this year include AI infrastructure unicorn Databricks , security provider Cyera , and the legal tech startups Harvey and Legora . No big slowdown in sight While prediction can be a fool’s game, there’s not much in the immediate set of indicators pointing to a slowdown in startups’ appetite for acquisition. Amid fierce competition for an edge in the AI race, well-funded startups commonly find it’s simply faster to buy another company than try to build out certain technologies themselves. Same goes for talent. Through acquihire transactions, startups can bring on board not just top-tier individuals but experienced teams with a track record of building impressive things together. Concentration of capital is another factor driving M&A deals. While overall startup funding has risen this year, it’s increasingly spread across a smaller pool of companies. That leaves one large cohort of startups struggling to raise funding while another has plentiful capital for acquisitions. Go-to-market expenses also factor into M&A considerations. A startup might produce a compelling offering in-house but find it costly to bring it to market. The process may look more feasible under the wing of a larger, more mature startup. Bottom line: Given the high number of willing sellers and well-funded buyers, expect the startup-to-startup acquisitions to continue. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 24 Aug 2026 16:15:25 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.8 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Inside The Private-Market Divide: EquityZen’s Phil Haslett On AI, SaaS And Secondaries https://news.crunchbase.com/liquidity/ai-ipo-ma-secondaries-haslett-equityzen/ Tue, 25 Aug 2026 11:00:33 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=93999 As startups stay private longer, the market for buying and selling shares in venture-backed companies before they go public has become increasingly active — and heated. EquityZen has been operating in that market since 2013. The New York-based company operates a marketplace for shares of privately held companies, giving employees and other shareholders a way to sell stock before a company goes public or is acquired. Morgan Stanley announced plans to acquire EquityZen in October 2025 and completed the deal in January 2026, bringing the company under the investment bank’s umbrella. Phil Haslett, co-founder and chief strategy officer of EquityZen. (Courtesy photo) Phil Haslett , who co-founded EquityZen and serves as its chief strategy officer, has had a front-row seat to the secondary market’s evolution. Crunchbase News spoke with Haslett about what secondary-market pricing says about today’s most sought-after startups, why AI companies are commanding premiums while many older startups trade at discounts, what the IPO market looks like beyond its biggest names, and why investors are taking a closer look at hard tech. The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Crunchbase News: The second quarter was one of the strongest venture-backed IPO quarters since 2021, but SpaceX drove much of that activity. If you remove SpaceX, how open is the IPO market for the typical late-stage startup? Phil Haslett: Generally, I’d say it’s better than it was three or six months ago. If you were a private late-stage technology company, you probably were going to wait until after SpaceX anyway, so that hurdle is gone. Tech markets are also doing well. The stock market is at an all-time high, and there’s been a strong recovery in tech stocks overall. I assume that we’re gearing up for a busier summer than usual. Another thing to consider is IPO performance beyond SpaceX. Some have had initial enthusiasm followed by a slowdown. Cerebras has come down a bit. So companies may see it as a good time to go public, while post-IPO performance has been, in a word, “meh.” But within AI, I think we’ve seen that there’s opportunity up and down the production curve — from energy for data centers, to the technology inside them, to orchestration of compute, to efficient spending on training and inference. There are a lot of interesting companies along that spectrum, and I think that bodes well for companies in the space that want to go public. A few companies entered your Top 20, including Figure AI , Project Prometheus , Redwood Materials and Scale AI . Does that reflect a durable shift away from traditional software, or are investors chasing a small group of scarce, high-profile hard-tech companies? Haslett: I think it reflects a thematic shift. The companies entering that list generally fall into AI infrastructure, space tech and robotics. If those are industries we think will have generational growth opportunities, the logical conclusion is that each sector will have winners. SpaceX gets people thinking about opportunities in space and space tech, and by extension defense tech. The same applies to AI infrastructure. If the market is that big, and we’ve seen companies go public over the last year or so, it stands to reason investors will be interested in other companies in that space. I think that’s more important than simply chasing scarce supply. These businesses tend to be more capital intensive and may take longer to reach predictable revenue than a traditional SaaS company. How are secondary investors underwriting them? Haslett: If a company needs more capital, investors have to decide whether the overall opportunity is big enough to justify waiting longer and having the company raise more. If you have to build a factory or get regulatory approval, that can delay the company’s ability to increase its valuation or reach an exit. Investors discount that into what they’re willing to pay. Secondary investors are making the same calculus as primary venture and growth investors, so you’d imagine much of that is already baked into headline valuations from primary raises. What’s changed is that capital-intensive companies now have more financing options. Five or six years ago, a battery company or new chip manufacturer might have had little choice but to raise equity. In 2026, more credit and asset-based financing options are available. That matters because if one of these companies underperforms or has a distressed asset sale, creditors and lenders get paid first. Secondary investors have to factor that in, too. EquityZen says the average transaction occurred at a 38% discount to the last funding round, while many AI transactions traded at premiums. What does that say about how bifurcated the private market has become? Haslett: I don’t know if it’s a mispricing. There are essentially two vintages of private companies right now. Some companies weren’t built AI-first and have had to adapt. Many raised during the go-go years of 2021, at very high valuations, and may not have raised since. They’ve had to rethink their strategies, which can slow growth and execution. That gets reflected in the discount. Then there’s a new wave of companies, from 2023 and beyond, that were built with an AI-first mentality. They started from a clean slate, may operate more efficiently, and have a cleaner story for the market. Some of those companies are raising rounds in quick succession at higher valuations. Secondary investors may pay a premium because they believe the company’s trajectory is clear and the next valuation increase could happen quickly. Airtable is an example from the 2021 cohort. It raised at roughly a $10 billion-plus valuation and just sold for substantially less. It’s still a good business, but when investors compare 20% growth with newer companies going from zero to hundreds of millions in revenue in just a few years, you can understand why their appetite changes. We may see more companies from that era sell for less than where they raised in 2021. Over the past few years, many private companies have conducted secondaries because they weren’t ready to go public. When should founders consider establishing a company-approved secondary program? Haslett: Historically, companies started thinking about liquidity programs after they’d been around five, six, or seven years, largely to reward employees for their patience and provide liquidity to early investors. Now we’re seeing younger companies engage in controlled liquidity and tender offers. One reason is talent retention. There are only so many engineers and data scientists, and companies need to compete for them. Secondary liquidity has become more normalized. More solutions are available than before. Morgan Stanley, for example, has significantly grown its tender-offer activity as investor interest and available tools have expanded. There’s also more investor appetite. Investors are increasingly willing to gain ownership through tender offers or secondary transactions. Five years ago, that was far less common. Right now, it’s a very founder- and employee-friendly environment, and investors are willing to support secondary liquidity because they want access. If markets turn, that pendulum could shift back. Nintendo didn’t design its Switch dock with travel in mind. Genki’s Covert Dock is a much smaller alternative my family has been using to connect our Switch to hotel TVs for years, but I’ve come to realize I much prefer having a stand for the console when using it this way. So when it came time to replace the Genki because Nintendo broke compatibility with the Switch 2, GuliKit’s updated travel dock seemed like a better fit for my needs. Like Nintendo’s, it provides a convenient place to perch the console while playing on a TV. It’s not perfect, but its few tradeoffs are easy to overlook given GuliKit’s solution is less than half the price of Genki’s. When I first unboxed the GuliKit Dock for Switch 2 , it felt like a bait and switch. Although it looks like it’s milled from a block of aluminum like my MacBook, the dock is actually an all-plastic affair that’s convincingly finished to look like metal. Picking it up for the first time was akin to grabbing an empty soda can you think is full. It’s surprisingly light, and while I was initially disappointed, I soon realized that was probably a good thing since I’m an over-packer who frequently deals with overweight baggage . GuliKit Dock for Switch 2 Where to Buy: $29.99 at Amazon The dock’s design — essentially a square puck with rounded corners — is larger than the Genki dock I used to travel with, but it’s by no means bulky or cumbersome. It’s wide enough to securely support the Switch when it’s docked (I actually wouldn’t want it any smaller), and it positions the console at a slight backwards angle that helps ensure it won’t fall off and face-plant even if accidentally bumped. A magnetic cover protects the USB-C connector when it’s not in use, but while the Switch is connected, the cover can be attached to the top of the dock where it doubles as a slightly taller backrest for the console. It’s a good idea, but one let down by relatively weak magnets. It doesn’t take much force to dislodge the cover, and I’ve already had it pop off on its own while buried in my backpack. Attaching the cover with a hinge held shut by a single strong magnet would have worked better, I think. On the underside of the dock are four rubber feet preventing it from sliding around and a three-position sliding switch that’s supposed to extend the USB-C connector to accommodate your console when it’s in a protective case. On the dock I tested, moving that switch to different positions only served to slightly change the angle of the USB-C connector by a few degrees, which doesn’t seem all that useful. On the back of the dock is a 4K/60Hz HDMI port, a USB-A port for charging accessories like a controller, and a USB-C port for connecting an adapter with up to 100W of power delivery. Having to supply your own power adapter is the biggest downside to choosing GuliKit’s dock over Genki’s that has one built-in and is designed to plug straight into an outlet. That could make GuliKit’s dock less appealing to some, but it’s not an issue for me given I already travel with multiple adapters that deliver the 60W the Switch 2 needs for its dock mode. Alongside the multiple ports on the back is also a small button that turns off dock mode and video output so the accessory only functions as a charger. GuliKit positions this feature as a way to charge and play the Switch in handheld mode without actually having to hold it. While the ergonomics of that approach seem less than ideal to me, disabling the dock mode does have the benefit of making the Switch charge a little faster if you’re in a rush to top off its battery. If you’re looking for the smallest possible way to connect your Switch 2 to a TV, you’re probably better off grabbing Genki’s or Jsaux’s accessories that incorporate a power adapter into their designs so all you need to provide is an HDMI and USB-C cable. GuliKit’s solution is slightly bulkier, but I really like that it replicates most of the functionality offered by the bundled Nintendo dock with a much smaller footprint. And it’s not just useful for traveling. If you want to connect your Switch 2 to TVs in multiple rooms around your home and don’t need an ethernet port, at $29.99 GuliKit’s is a much cheaper alternative to Nintendo’s $124.99 dock set , even when factoring in the added cost of an HDMI cable and 60W adapter. Nintendo didn’t design its Switch dock with travel in mind. Genki’s Covert Dock is a much smaller alternative my family has been using to connect our Switch to hotel TVs for years, but I’ve come to realize I much prefer having a stand for the console when using it this way. So when it came time to replace the Genki because Nintendo broke compatibility with the Switch 2, GuliKit’s updated travel dock seemed like a better fit for my needs. Like Nintendo’s, it provides a convenient place to perch the console while playing on a TV. It’s not perfect, but its few tradeoffs are easy to overlook given GuliKit’s solution is less than half the price of Genki’s. When I first unboxed the GuliKit Dock for Switch 2 , it felt like a bait and switch. Although it looks like it’s milled from a block of aluminum like my MacBook, the dock is actually an all-plastic affair that’s convincingly finished to look like metal. Picking it up for the first time was akin to grabbing an empty soda can you think is full. It’s surprisingly light, and while I was initially disappointed, I soon realized that was probably a good thing since I’m an over-packer who frequently deals with overweight baggage . GuliKit Dock for Switch 2 Where to Buy: $29.99 at Amazon The dock’s design — essentially a square puck with rounded corners — is larger than the Genki dock I used to travel with, but it’s by no means bulky or cumbersome. It’s wide enough to securely support the Switch when it’s docked (I actually wouldn’t want it any smaller), and it positions the console at a slight backwards angle that helps ensure it won’t fall off and face-plant even if accidentally bumped. A magnetic cover protects the USB-C connector when it’s not in use, but while the Switch is connected, the cover can be attached to the top of the dock where it doubles as a slightly taller backrest for the console. It’s a good idea, but one let down by relatively weak magnets. It doesn’t take much force to dislodge the cover, and I’ve already had it pop off on its own while buried in my backpack. Attaching the cover with a hinge held shut by a single strong magnet would have worked better, I think. On the underside of the dock are four rubber feet preventing it from sliding around and a three-position sliding switch that’s supposed to extend the USB-C connector to accommodate your console when it’s in a protective case. On the dock I tested, moving that switch to different positions only served to slightly change the angle of the USB-C connector by a few degrees, which doesn’t seem all that useful. On the back of the dock is a 4K/60Hz HDMI port, a USB-A port for charging accessories like a controller, and a USB-C port for connecting an adapter with up to 100W of power delivery. Having to supply your own power adapter is the biggest downside to choosing GuliKit’s dock over Genki’s that has one built-in and is designed to plug straight into an outlet. That could make GuliKit’s dock less appealing to some, but it’s not an issue for me given I already travel with multiple adapters that deliver the 60W the Switch 2 needs for its dock mode. Alongside the multiple ports on the back is also a small button that turns off dock mode and video output so the accessory only functions as a charger. GuliKit positions this feature as a way to charge and play the Switch in handheld mode without actually having to hold it. While the ergonomics of that approach seem less than ideal to me, disabling the dock mode does have the benefit of making the Switch charge a little faster if you’re in a rush to top off its battery. If you’re looking for the smallest possible way to connect your Switch 2 to a TV, you’re probably better off grabbing Genki’s or Jsaux’s accessories that incorporate a power adapter into their designs so all you need to provide is an HDMI and USB-C cable. GuliKit’s solution is slightly bulkier, but I really like that it replicates most of the functionality offered by the bundled Nintendo dock with a much smaller footprint. And it’s not just useful for traveling. If you want to connect your Switch 2 to TVs in multiple rooms around your home and don’t need an ethernet port, at $29.99 GuliKit’s is a much cheaper alternative to Nintendo’s $124.99 dock set , even when factoring in the added cost of an HDMI cable and 60W adapter. Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge ]]> Andrew J. Nintendo didn’t design its Switch dock with travel in mind. Genki’s Covert Dock is a much smaller alternative my family has been using to connect our Switch to hotel TVs for years, but I’ve come to realize I much prefer having a stand for the console when using it this way. So when it came time to replace the Genki because Nintendo broke compatibility with the Switch 2, GuliKit’s updated travel dock seemed like a better fit for my needs. Like Nintendo’s, it provides a convenient place to perch the console while playing on a TV. It’s not perfect, but its few tradeoffs are easy to overlook given GuliKit’s solution is less than half the price of Genki’s. When I first unboxed the GuliKit Dock for Switch 2 , it felt like a bait and switch. Although it looks like it’s milled from a block of aluminum like my MacBook, the dock is actually an all-plastic affair that’s convincingly finished to look like metal. Picking it up for the first time was akin to grabbing an empty soda can you think is full. It’s surprisingly light, and while I was initially disappointed, I soon realized that was probably a good thing since I’m an over-packer who frequently deals with overweight baggage . GuliKit Dock for Switch 2 Where to Buy: $29.99 at Amazon The dock’s design — essentially a square puck with rounded corners — is larger than the Genki dock I used to travel with, but it’s by no means bulky or cumbersome. It’s wide enough to securely support the Switch when it’s docked (I actually wouldn’t want it any smaller), and it positions the console at a slight backwards angle that helps ensure it won’t fall off and face-plant even if accidentally bumped. A magnetic cover protects the USB-C connector when it’s not in use, but while the Switch is connected, the cover can be attached to the top of the dock where it doubles as a slightly taller backrest for the console. It’s a good idea, but one let down by relatively weak magnets. It doesn’t take much force to dislodge the cover, and I’ve already had it pop off on its own while buried in my backpack. Attaching the cover with a hinge held shut by a single strong magnet would have worked better, I think. On the underside of the dock are four rubber feet preventing it from sliding around and a three-position sliding switch that’s supposed to extend the USB-C connector to accommodate your console when it’s in a protective case. On the dock I tested, moving that switch to different positions only served to slightly change the angle of the USB-C connector by a few degrees, which doesn’t seem all that useful. On the back of the dock is a 4K/60Hz HDMI port, a USB-A port for charging accessories like a controller, and a USB-C port for connecting an adapter with up to 100W of power delivery. Having to supply your own power adapter is the biggest downside to choosing GuliKit’s dock over Genki’s that has one built-in and is designed to plug straight into an outlet.
